articles.title: Background checks should be mandatory for Hill staff, Cammack says
articles.description: When you land a job in most parts of the federal government or the private sector, you can expect a fairly standard step — a criminal background check. Want to work for your member of Congress? No background check necessary. Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., hopes to change that. A resolution introduced by Cammack would amend House rules to force employees to undergo criminal background checks conducted by Capitol Police. It also would require them to disclose any payments they may have received from foreign governments in the three years leading up to their hiring. “This is the least the House should be doing,” Cammack said in an interview, describing it as a basic step to ensure public servants are “acting in the best interests of the taxpayers” who fund their paychecks. “People are absolutely gobsmacked when they find out that that is not a standard practice in the House,” she said. Right now, members of Congress can opt to run checks on the staff they hire in their offices, but it isn’t mandatory. Capitol Police declined to provide numbers on how many they conducted in 2025 across the legislative branch. “We’ve had members say that they have found things like domestic abuse, harassment, battery, things like that,” Cammack said. With more than 400 member offices spread across the House, the Capitol can sometimes feel like a collection of fiefdoms, each with its own hiring practices and internal norms. While the House already has a separate standardized process for issuing security clearances to staffers who handle secret information, it’s capped at two staffers per office. Adding criminal background checks for everyone could help identify red flags, Cammack argues, especially at a time when Congress is grappling with how it handles sexual harassment and foreign influence. “There are things in people’s records, in their backgrounds, that maybe would have indicated that this person has a problem or could potentially have a problem,” said Cammack, who once worked as a congressional staffer herself for former Rep. Ted Yoho, R-Fla. Her resolution, which would need just a majority vote in the House for adoption because it applies only to that chamber, has seen no action since she introduced it last summer. But as she helps lead a different effort to overhaul sexual harassment rules and training on the Hill, she views the two topics as connected. “It’s an interesting dynamic now as we are really seeing the sexual misconduct culture get a very bright light shone on it,” she said. A clean slate? Background checks are “desperately needed” for certain situations, particularly when it comes to jobs that handle sensitive information, agrees Reginald Darby, who works as federal legislative director at the Clean Slate Initiative. He’s not against Cammack’s proposal — but his group wants to see broader legislative action that could help some of the estimated 1 in 3 adults around the country who have an arrest or conviction record. articles.title: Trump’s funding cancellation violates budget law, GAO says
articles.description: The Government Accountability Office reaffirmed its opinion Tuesday that “pocket rescissions” are illegal, dealing a modest blow to President Donald Trump’s announcement last week of plans to cancel $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress. In a letter to congressional leaders, the GAO —the investigative arm of Congress — doubled down on its position that the administration would violate a 1974 budget law by trying to rescind, or cancel, funding that lawmakers had already appropriated in the closing days of the fiscal year, which ends Wednesday. That short timeline gives Congress virtually no time to act on the request as the funding is set to expire. “Any withholding of appropriated funds beyond their date of expiration, regardless of size, subverts both the constitutional process for enacting federal law and Congress’s constitutional power of the purse,” the GAO wrote. “The President may not force the expiration of budget authority Congress has already enacted and did not rescind.”; The GAO opinion follows Trump’s submittal of a “special message” to Congress Friday laying out plans to cancel $810 million in funding for health, education and other programs. Related: White House cancels health, education funds approved by Congress; Under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act, the president may send a request to Congress to cancel funding and withhold the funding for up to 45 days while lawmakers consider the request. Congress may approve the request, reject it or amend it. With the House on recess until after the elections, there is no practical way for the House to consider the request before the fiscal year ends. But the opinion is unlikely to have any practical effect unless the GAO takes the administration to court. White House officials have said they do not feel bound by the GAO, which is a legislative agency outside the purview of the executive branch. And White House budget director Russ Vought immediately dismissed the opinion in a post on X, while accusing the GAO of acting with partisan, political motive. “GAO has become hyper partisan and Congress recently attempted to cut their spending because of it,” Vought wrote. “They make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.”; The pocket rescission has drawn condemnation from Democrats and some Republicans, including Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who have vowed to fight what they called an illegal action. articles.description: The Senate passed legislation that would amend the Clean Air Act to ensure states would not be penalized for conducting prescribed burns intended to prevent larger, uncontrolled wildfires by unanimous consent on Tuesday. Under current law, states are required to meet air quality standards for particulate matter pollution. Controlled burns can increase this pollution, and while these are technically “exceptional events” that wouldn’t count toward whether a state is in compliance, states have said they face a high administrative burden of proof. Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, the bill’s lead sponsor, described the measure as “one of the most effective ways” to reduce hazardous fuels and prevent catastrophic wildfires. “With every passing day, the threat to our communities, our lands, and our very lives grows more severe. That is why it makes no sense to leave a critical tool like controlled burns off the table,” he said on the Senate floor on Tuesday. He said the data is clear that wildfire containment and prevention is “far more successful in areas where prescribed burns took place,” yet states can face regulatory consequences for doing so. The measure would require the EPA to propose revisions to regulations that would make it easier for states to demonstrate a prescribed fire is an exceptional event. Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said on the floor that while his constituents would have once opposed prescribed burns, many now support the practice with the hope that it may help avert events such as the 2020 Labor Day fires in Oregon that burned more than 1 million acres. “Prescribed burns are, along with thinning and mowing, significant ways to reduce the fuel load and reduce the devastation when there is a fire,” said Merkley. “They say an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. That’s a pretty good foundation for a bill.”; Merkley also highlighted a provision in the bill that would establish a grant program to prevent, control or abate wildfire smoke hazards in community buildings, including schools. The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved the measure earlier in September on a 19-0 vote. It now faces negotiations with the House, which passed a competing bill in April that would also change how prescribed burns are treated under the CAA. Introduced by Rep. articles.title: How is ‘Mean Girls’ like gerrymandering? Ask these former Hill staffers
articles.description: On the surface, it wouldn’t seem like an early-aughts teen comedy has much in common with the drawing of congressional maps. Don’t tell that to Rory Riley Topping and Josh Rultenberg, who spend a good chunk of their new book referencing “Mean Girls.” The authors of “Draw the Line in Ohio” are on a mission to break down gerrymandering for a wider audience, one “get in, loser” at a time. “People who care about politics, they can nerd out,” Topping said, but most people’s “eyes glaze over” when you talk about redistricting. The way she sees it, Regina George — and other pop culture touchstones — can help. “I am a Bravo super-fan. So yes, I am happy to include references to things like ‘Vanderpump Rules’ any chance I can get,” she added. Rultenberg said he wasn’t worried about diluting or cheapening a topic he sees as serious, even when the stakes are high. “If we can get people in the front door by talking about Stefon on ‘Saturday Night Live,’ all of a sudden they’re smiling before they realize that they’re probably going to be crying about what’s happening in this country,” he said. Gerrymandering is a key driver of political corruption, the book argues, beyond its more obvious role in shaping which party controls Congress. The co-authors share something else — they’re both former congressional staffers. Topping worked for Republicans as staff director for a House Veterans’ Affairs subcommittee in the early 2010s, while Rultenberg briefly served as communications director for Ohio Democratic Rep. Emilia Sykes until this summer. What was it like to collaborate across the aisle on such a politically charged topic? articles.title: Bipartisan Senate duo drops new data center bills

One bill would establish a program within the Department of Energy to give communities access to technical expertise to better understand the costs and benefits of proposed data center developments. articles.title: Centrist Dem’s Supreme Court plan boosts momentum for revamp

The group says it also wants to inject ideas to overhaul the court — including legislation to set an 18-year term limit and an enforceable ethics code — into the party’s conversations leading up to the 2028 presidential race. “This is one of those things that we think can and should be a part of the 2028 discussion, and those folks who are running should be asked about whether they would champion Supreme Court reform,” Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at Third Way, said in an interview. Key Democratic groups have increasingly been coalescing around ideas to overhaul the court’s structure and policing in light of accusations of growing partisanship and corruption among justices. In June, a number of key Democratic House caucus leaders, including the Congressional Progressive Caucus, released their own resolution calling for term limits for justices and a code of ethics. “We think that the center left has been remiss in not being forward enough on reform proposals that would make our system work better for people, which is why some folks have gone to the further left,” Erickson said. Third Way cited public opinion polling from both the Brennan Center for Justice and FOX News indicating more than 70 percent of respondents favored term limits for justices. An 18-year cycle would ensure the appointment of two justices every presidential term. The group also wants legislation to hold justices accountable for ethics violations. Still, the group’s recommendations are meant “to show that the center left can also be bold and be addressing systemic problems to appeal to voters and their level of anxiety and anger about what's happening right now,” Erickson said.

articles.title: As Congress leans on ‘pro formas,’ bills become law without Trump signature

That dynamic was on display in July, when a blockbuster housing overhaul and a lesser-known measure expanding disaster relief payments to farmers quietly became law without the pomp and circumstance sometimes seen in presidential bill signings. The two laws were enacted through what’s known as the “10-day rule.” The Constitution says that bills become law after 10 days, excluding Sundays, without a presidential signature — as long as Congress has not adjourned. Pro formas, brief meetings of the House or Senate during which business is not usually conducted, allow the chambers to stay in session. The pair of bills enacted this summer appear to have little in common except this: Each was sponsored by members of the president’s party. Congressional experts say President Donald Trump’s penchant for using his political leverage, particularly against fellow GOP lawmakers, is among the driving forces for withholding a presidential signature. “It’s not so much maybe about the actual policy of it, but about denying House and Senate Republicans the optics of a big bill signing,” said SoRelle Wyckoff Gaynor, assistant professor of public policy and politics at the University of Virginia. That, she added, “is a powerful tool that really only Trump can wield.”; In the case of the housing law, Trump declared he would not sign the bill because he was frustrated that the Senate had not passed an election security bill that would require voters to prove their citizenship. He was responding to Altman’s comments to Decoded by POLITICO that people “should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”; Pressed further on whether he agreed with Altman’s premise, Thompson replied, “No, I think we have to work harder to prevent any bad things from happening."; Altman’s comments come in the wake of increased panic over the risks of catastrophic destruction from AI, with many industry leaders and experts arguing that guardrails are needed on the technology to prevent it from spinning out of human control. The executives of major AI labs and tech companies gathered at the White House last week to discuss solutions with President Donald Trump, who believes overregulating AI will have national security repercussions. The group ended up signing a “morally binding” AI accord that critics say won’t do enough to prevent a worst-case scenario. Thompson noted Monday he believes that AI will bring “tremendous solutions,” specifically in regards to finding cures for health issues like cancer and Alzheimer's disease. But he also said AI has to be led with “principle” — comparing it to how he addressed digital assets in a bill to regulate the cryptocurrency industry, which he worked on as chair of the Agriculture Committee. “The first principle is ‘do no harm.’ So we need to protect consumers, and that means, I think, building some guardrails — some guidelines — to do that,” Thompson said. articles.title: ‘Save the Senate’? Duo floats big changes to chamber rules
articles.description: Two years ago, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., published a book about restoring the so-called talking filibuster and repairing what he describes as a “broken” system in the Senate. Now he’s forming an unlikely duo with Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to push a sweeping proposal to overhaul the chamber’s rules. “America today is larger, busier and more complex than the America our Founding Fathers designed the Senate and its rules to govern,” the pair wrote in a seven-page document they released Thursday. Daines, who previously served as the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, is retiring at the end of his term in January, while Merkley is up for reelection this year. “We’re sharing our plan now, before the midterm elections, because these reforms are needed no matter who wins in November,” they wrote in an op-ed in the Washington Post. They envision spending less time on cloture votes, as well as setting up a fast-track process for certain bills. In some ways, that would move the chamber closer to how things are done in the House, where bipartisan bills routinely pass quickly on suspension with a two-thirds vote. The Senate has been “diminished as an institution,” according to their proposal, thanks in part to “the enormous workload and today’s political polarization.”; “In the coming few years it will either be further paralyzed by partisan politics and demands — breaking the few norms that remain — or it will rebound to an institution where robust debate and bipartisan policymaking both flourish,” they wrote. They want to eliminate cloture votes on motions to proceed, amendments and nominations. The intervening day before a vote to break a filibuster would also be eliminated, with debate time condensed. Cloture votes have come to eat up more time than anyone anticipated, they argue. “Cloture was created in 1917 as a tool for the Senate to end filibusters and start voting. But the 60-vote threshold generally required for a cloture motion to pass is now deliberately abused to slow down the legislative process and delay voting on big issues,” they wrote in the Post op-ed. While some see the Senate as the infamous “cooling saucer” that is meant to slow things down by design, Merkley and Daines want to move the chamber more in line with its faster-moving cousin, at least in one way. “A Senate version of the House suspension calendar” would allow certain bills that have advanced out of committee to pass on the floor with two-thirds of senators in support, and “robustly bipartisan” bills could get an even smoother glide path with a majority threshold. Replacing Alito during the Trump administration could mean cementing the court’s current controlling 6-3 conservative bloc for years to come and would give Trump his fourth pick on the court. “I intend to stick around through this term,” Alito said in the Bloomberg interview released Tuesday. articles.title: Retiring Durbin stepped up to the plate time and again for baseball
articles.description: Long before Illinois Sen. Richard J. Durbin climbed the ranks of Democratic leadership, he took an interest in the politics of baseball. Back in 1989, when Durbin was representing a Springfield-based district in the House, he lamented changes that were being proposed to the professional ranks of America’s national pastime, including railing against the potential switch to aluminum bats in the major leagues. “Designated hitters, plastic grass, uniforms that look like pajamas, chicken clowns dancing on the baselines, and, of course, the most heinous sacrilege, lights in Wrigley Field,” Durbin said in a floor speech, spelling out various indignities that already befallen the game. He’s retiring from the Senate. What will happen to his ‘dream’? But it was the potential switch from wood to aluminum – an idea ultimately abandoned – that precipitated Durbin’s remarks. “I don’t want to hear about saving trees. Any tree in America would gladly give its life for a day of glory at home plate,” the then-congressman said. “I don’t know if it will take a constitutional amendment to keep the baseball traditions alive, but if we forsake the great Americana of broken-bat singles and pine tar, we certainly will have lost our way as a nation.”; It’s far from the only issue related to baseball that the retiring Senate minority whip has engaged in over his more than four decades in Congress. In 2019, he teamed up with fellow Illinois Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth to push for Major League Baseball to extend the use of netting designed to shield fans from foul balls. “With more foul balls being hit at high speeds into the stands than ever before, it was imperative for MLB to address ballpark safety at the Winter Meetings,” the senators said in a statement after the league announced a plan of action. “Extending protective netting well beyond the end of each dugout will make the ballpark a safer place for fans to enjoy a game.”; Durbin later followed up on the issue, joining with MLB to announce that extended netting was coming to minor league stadiums, as well. “We are building on the progress made over the last three years so we can also attend minor league games with our kids and grandkids without fear for their safety, no matter where we’re seated,” he said in a 2022 statement. As Durbin nears retirement, Major League Baseball appears headed toward another work stoppage after the World Series this month, evoking memories of an earlier lockout that delayed the start of the regular 2022 season. Amid that labor dispute, Durbin at one point threatened to go after the sport’s antitrust exemption. “After almost 100 days of the MLB lockout, it’s time to reconsider MLB’s special antitrust exemption, which allows them to act as a lawful monopoly,” he posted on social media on March 9, 2022. “Fans across America deserve better.”; MLB club owners and the players’ union reached an agreement to end the lockout the following day.

articles.title: Bipartisan group of senators demands Trump rescind Russian diesel deal
articles.description: A bipartisan group of senators urged President Donald Trump on Tuesday to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, amid bubbling anger on Capitol Hill about Trump’s announcement. In a letter sent to the White House, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the senators warned that the president’s deal with Russia will not “achieve just ends” or benefit Americans. “Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war,” wrote the lawmakers, led by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). “This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded.”; On Sunday, a smaller group of senators called on the president to “immediately reverse course” on the plan in a statement. Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) — who signed on to both — said Sunday there may be “a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law.”; The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump announced in a social media post on Friday that Russia would “immediately supply” diesel fuel to global markets — including potentially the U.S. — to help relieve high prices driven, in part, by the ongoing war with Iran. Though Trump has repeatedly defended the U.S.’s actions against Iran, on Saturday he demanded an end to Ukrainian drone strikes that have crippled Russian oil refineries that he argues have caused the record-high oil prices. The senators on Tuesday argued that the deal with Russia will have a “negligible impact” on fuel prices while providing Putin with “more fuel to finance his war machine” as Russia continues its “brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians.”; The deal with Russia is a sharp pivot from a sweeping sanctions package signed into law last month. That legislation — championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) — was meant to deplete Moscow’s resources by targeting Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of oil tankers. It drew widespread bipartisan support in both chambers of Congress. Senators on Tuesday referenced the package as they condemned Putin as a “tyrant.”; “For decades, America has stood as the bastion of freedom against tyranny, and American presidents have embodied our nation’s resistance to tyrants. Putin is a tyrant,” the letter reads. “Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. articles.title: Bipartisan duo maps out AI safety plan as congressional action lags
articles.description: A bipartisan Senate duo is urging Trump national security officials to “bring its full capacities to bear” to stave off threats posed by artificial intelligence — sooner rather than later. Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, and Republican South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds, who serves on the Senate Armed Services Cybersecurity Subcommittee, are calling for a full government response to a growing number of cybersecurity breaches. “Recent AI security incidents should serve as a warning,” the senators wrote in a Tuesday letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and White House Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. “Advanced AI agents have escaped testing environments, bypassed safeguards, and gained unauthorized access to real-world systems owned by government agencies and private organizations.”; Spokespeople for Clayton and Kratsios did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Their letter comes as lawmakers struggle to hash out what legislation on AI safety, if any, might look like. Members are currently in recess ahead of the November elections, and there’s little hope progress can be made by the year’s end. But those lawmakers who have been engaged on the topic for years now have mapped out administrative actions the Trump administration could move on now, without waiting on Congress. The Cantwell and Rounds priorities include: strengthening federal AI safety and security standards at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST; expanding independent testing capabilities at the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, Department of Energy and the national labs; and working with the tech industry to develop and deploy defensive AI tools. Specifically, the senators wrote, new NIST standards should address the risks posed by advanced AI capabilities, including the “potential misuse by malicious actors” to conduct sophisticated cyberattacks, automate attacks at scale and agents that threaten external systems and critical infrastructure. They also said the federal government capacity should be complemented by universities and other research organizations, as well as by private sector, third-party evaluators. Finally, they point to ways the government could use existing programs at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency to work with AI labs to help detect threats and reinforce vulnerable systems.

articles.title: Omar home search raises fears about election-season probes
articles.description: A search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home has sent shockwaves through electoral politics weeks before the midterms, as experts said it appeared to flout longstanding norms meant to keep prosecutors out of elections. While the Minnesota Democrat herself has been on a glide path to reelection in a deep-blue district, some worry it could set a wider precedent for how the Trump administration handles investigations of other politicians. Homeland Security Investigations agents carried out a federal search warrant of her D.C. home on Monday, according to Omar and officials. It comes as Republicans face an uphill battle to retain control of the House and after President Donald Trump has criticized Omar for years and publicly accused her of immigration fraud. The timing of the search raises serious questions, according to several experts. David Sklansky, a professor at Stanford Law School and former federal prosecutor, said the search, even though it was conducted by Homeland Security officials, may have run afoul of two Justice Department policies, one formal and one informal. “There’s lots of reasons to suspect this is politically motivated, and there’s very little evidence that it isn’t politically motivated,” Sklansky said. The Justice Department manual states that federal officials should never direct the timing of an investigative step “for the purpose” of affecting an election and directs agents to consult the Public Integrity Section if an impact is possible. The Public Integrity Section normally handles cases involving public corruption and elected officials and has faced controversy in the second Trump administration. Beyond the manual, Sklansky said the DOJ has an informal “60-day rule” where investigators are discouraged from taking actions close to an election. A 2018 inspector general report that criticized the handling of the probe of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in the days leading up to the 2016 election noted that there was no written guidance for such situations. Gregg Nunziata, executive director for the Society for the Rule of Law and former DOJ counsel, said the search could undermine trust in the DOJ when it files a case. “Congressmen, senators, members of an administration — they do break the law, they’re not above the law. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, imploring Iowans to “defy history” and help him preserve the GOP majority. Turnout is lower in midterm elections, and the president’s party tends to lose seats, Johnson said at the Friday rally, but “we cannot risk that.” Rattling off details about his party’s slim margins and historical statistics, Johnson urged the Republican faithful gathered at the GOP “battlestation” in the eastern part of the state to do everything they could. “Let’s win this race by more than six votes this time,” Johnson said, a reference to Miller-Meeks’ 2020 victory. Inside Elections rates the 1st District and Republican Rep. Zach Nunn’s 3rd District as “tilt Democratic.” The race to replace retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst is rated “tilt Republican.” The open seat gubernatorial race is rated “tilt Democratic,” which would be a flip of a state President Donald Trump carried by 13 percent in 2024 and also won handily in 2020 and 2016. That’s why Iowa is ground zero for control of Congress. Interviews with Iowans in small cities, college towns and rural areas last week revealed an engaged electorate frustrated with partisan politics and hoping for candidates who will work on local issues like water quality, education and gas prices, which were $4.29 a gallon for regular at most pumps last week. Diesel was more than $6 at many stations. The conversations with more than 75 voters across more than 1,000 miles also suggested Iowans relish the color purple and bipartisanship. It’s a place feeling the pain of the war in Iran and tariffs, and where Trump’s name draws mixed reactions. articles.title: Whatley campaign is currently dark on TV as GOP groups retreat from North Carolina
articles.description: Michael Whatley’s campaign has temporarily gone dark in North Carolina. The Republican Senate nominee does not currently have future linear TV ad reservations booked in the race, a highly unusual move less than three weeks before Election Day in a state that was once considered a top GOP priority. Whatley’s last broadcast TV ad aired one week ago, according to tracking firm AdImpact. The pause comes as Republicans and major outside GOP groups, including Senate Leadership Fund, disinvest from the state in an acknowledgment of the difficulty of beating Democratic nominee Roy Cooper, the former North Carolina governor, in November. “It’s a temporary pause and we’ll be back on the air shortly with our closing message that may or may not ask voters why does our elderly opponent refuse to answer basic questions about his health and ability to serve in the U.S. Senate,” Whatley spokesperson DJ Griffin said in a statement. “We are confident we have the resources needed to win the only poll that matters — Election Day in November.”; Cooper’s campaign, by contrast, has $7.4 million in future TV ad reservations, in addition to $11.2 million from outside groups. Republican outside groups have just $4.7 million reserved, giving Democrats a nearly 4 to 1 advantage in future TV ad spending, according to an analysis of AdImpact data. The move by Whatley’s campaign is rare this close to the election, a period when candidates typically ramp up their advertising as voters begin casting ballots. “It was always going to be a tough seat for Rs to hold,” said Doug Heye, a longtime GOP strategist who is from North Carolina. “Trump’s numbers are in the tank and Cooper is a good candidate who has won statewide. This is what was always going to happen.”; Cooper, who has repeatedly led Whatley in public polling and candidate fundraising, enters the final stretch of the campaign as the clear front-runner over Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee and the handpicked candidate of President Donald Trump. A spokesperson for Cooper sharply rebutted the Whatley campaign’s characterizations about the Democrat’s health. “These are more desperate lies from a desperate candidate,” Kate Smart said in a statement. “Roy Cooper has held over 350 events over the course of this campaign, is in excellent health and will obviously serve his full term.”; Major outside groups on both sides have already begun retreating from North Carolina. The GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund paused its spending in the state earlier this month, while other Republican groups, including Old North Action, have also pulled back. Democrats are increasingly bullish on Cooper’s chances of flipping the seat — one of four pickups the party needs to win back the Senate, assuming it defends all of its current seats. The Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC has also started pausing its spending in North Carolina, increasingly turning their attention to fund other competitive Senate races.

articles.description: The Supreme Court on Wednesday grappled with how far a law Congress passed to cover video rentals in the 1980s should stretch to cover the modern advertising-supported internet. The case turns on the justices’ interpretation of the Video Privacy Protection Act, first passed in 1988 and last amended in 2013, and the protection it is meant to provide for consumers’ information when they rent or purchase videos. The law protects “consumers” of video content from having private information about their viewing habits from being disclosed without their permission. Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh, along with other members of the panel, weighed how to handle the text of a decades-old statute when technology has massively changed in the interim. “Isn’t there a concern about repurposing a statute that was really about public disclosure of what individuals viewed into a statute that regulates data sharing for targeted advertising on the internet?” Kavanaugh asked. The case argued Wednesday started with a lawsuit from Michael Salazar when he signed up for a newsletter from a college sports website called 247Sports.com, an entity owned by Paramount. The company provided his data to Meta for advertising, and Salazar argued that transaction violated the privacy law. A federal trial judge found that although the website provided videos, the newsletter Salazar signed up for did not qualify him as a “consumer” under the law because the newsletter was not the kind of media the law covered. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit agreed, and Salazar appealed to the justices. Congress first passed the law after reporters published the video rental history of the late Judge Robert Bork during his failed nomination to the Supreme Court in 1987. The law makes a “video tape services provider” liable for damages if it provides personal information about a “consumer” of its products to a third party. A ruling either way could affect a wide swath of lawsuits brought over privacy concerns over personal information shared with internet giants. Hammack, attorney for Salazar, argued that Congress wrote a statute that it intended to apply in the future, even if technology changed. Companies providing video services could just get permission to share data from their consumers and avoid facing lawsuits, he said. “Congress was very concerned about consent and the consumer controlling the disclosure of personally identifiable information,” Hammack said. Hammack also pointed out that Congress left much of the law unchanged when it updated parts of it in 2013, indicating that it intended it to still apply. articles.description: President Donald Trump’s new top congressional liaison has entered the job in limbo, with control of the House and Senate too close to call and a boss who could be slowed by a slew of investigations over his final two years in office if Democrats take the majority in one or both chambers. Trump on Saturday announced that Katie Bailey would become his legislative affairs director. She most recently had been a top deputy in that office. Forecasting the White House’s legislative agenda and how successful she might be likely will have to wait after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Maxine Waters, 88, who has spent decades on the committee, faces a challenge from Rep. Sean Casten, 54, and a potential bid from Rep. Bill Foster, 71, a more moderate panel member. And Rep. A spokesperson for Beatty said in a statement she’d be voting for Waters as chair. Waters, a resistance icon and accomplished legislator, meanwhile, is already shoring up support. “Unless there is an individual who brings the unrivaled experience and tantalizing toughness of Maxine Waters, I look forward to supporting her,” Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a member of both Financial Services and the Congressional Black Caucus, said in a statement. The 50-plus member CBC is likely to bolster Waters’ bid, and Waters could also leverage her Los Angeles-area seat for support from the 43 Democrats in California’s congressional delegation. Beatty is also a CBC member. Waters and her team have also been making calls this week to recruit members to whip for her, including moderate Rep. Josh Gottheimer and progressive Rep. articles.title: Authorities investigate ‘suspicious substances’ mailed to congressional offices
articles.description: Authorities are investigating letters containing “suspicious substances” sent to multiple Capitol Hill offices, according to a notice sent to senior congressional staff. “Law enforcement officials are working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations,” says a memo from the Senate Sergeant at Arms and obtained by POLITICO. The Capitol Police, FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are involved in the probe, according to the notice, which said additional letters have been mailed to other addresses across the U.S., including lawmakers’ state and district offices. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) was one of the lawmakers sent mail containing the substance. It was identified by law enforcement before reaching the office. "The Senator and staff were not in immediate danger," according to a statement from Murphy's spokesperson. The office of Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) was also notified by law enforcement that suspicious mail was intercepted by USPS. A separate notice sent to House staffers Thursday identified the substance in the letters as a “suspicious white powder” and said that no House members "have been identified as recipients at this time."; The message from the House Sergeant at Arms urged staff to "remain vigilant and follow safe mail handling procedures to help protect staff from potentially harmful materials."; It is unclear if any of the suspicious letters reached Capitol Hill. Letters and packages sent to congressional offices are subject to off-site screening under a system established after the 2001 anthrax attacks. The memo includes a photo of one of the suspicious envelopes and warns staff to keep an eye out for warning signs, such as messy handwriting or postmarks that do not match the return address. The memo was first reported by Bloomberg Government. Suspicious letters were also sent to state election offices and election officials, according to a joint statement Wednesday from the National Association of Secretaries of State and National Association of State Election Directors. They said they are working with law enforcement to protect “personnel and facilities” and that contingency plans and security measures are in place to respond to threats “while maintaining essential election operations.”; House and Senate mail is processed in two separate Maryland facilities where materials are screened, irradiated and tested for a variety of substances before they are sent to the Capitol complex — a process that can add as much as two weeks to delivery. The process has proved effective in the past, catching a string of suspected explosive devices sent to prominent Democrats in 2018 and a ricin-laced envelope sent to Sen. articles.title: Bipartisan House group urges Trump to enforce Russia sanctions, scrap diesel deal
articles.description: A bipartisan group of House lawmakers urged President Donald Trump to follow through on the Russia sanctions law he signed last month, warning on Thursday against giving Moscow economic relief as a key enforcement deadline approaches. In a letter led by Rep. Jim Costa (D-Calif.) and shared first with POLITICO, 22 House lawmakers asked Trump to fully implement the sanctions law named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham by Oct. 18 and scrap his administration’s recent Russian diesel deal. “As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war,” the lawmakers wrote in the letter sent to Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The House lawmakers called for the Trump administration to apply sanctions “to their fullest extent and without delay” against Russian officials, oligarchs and banks financing the war — as well as the foreign banks, shadow fleet operators and intermediaries helping Moscow evade restrictions. Included among the lawmakers who signed Thursday’s letter are Republican Reps. Don Bacon (Neb.), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.), Michael McCaul (Texas), Dan Newhouse (Wash.) and Joe Wilson (S.C.), along with Democrats including Reps. Steny Hoyer (Md.), Marcy Kaptur (Ohio) and Jared Golden (Maine) — among others. The lawmakers' demands Thursday add to growing bipartisan pressure on Trump over his deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, after the president announced on Friday that Russia would supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to the “American and Global Marketplace.”; They also requested details on which sanctions and tariffs will take effect before Oct. 18, whether any provisions will be delayed or waived, and how the administration reconciles the diesel license with the existing statutory ban on Russian energy imports. “Putin has repeatedly shown that he responds to pressure, not goodwill,” the House members wrote. “This will make clear that American resolve is bipartisan and durable, and that the cost of continuing this war will only grow until Russia comes to the negotiating table. The White House, the State Department and the Treasury Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Trump defended the agreement Tuesday as “a deal for the world,” saying the diesel would enter global markets rather than go directly to the U.S. The move comes as the president scrambles to try to bring down fuel prices ahead of the midterms. The Iran war — now in its seventh month — has contributed to the surge in costs, with the average price of diesel peaking at a record $6.53 per gallon in September, according to AAA.
